newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Slow economy, new plant hits Australia's Fairfax.
newsitem.headline: Slow economy, new plant hits Australia's Fairfax.

text.p: Australia's oldest newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd reported a 17-percent fall in annual profits on Wednesday, blaming a slow economy and higher costs from a new printing plant for the slide.

Fairfax, about 22-percent owned by New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd, said pre-abnormals net profit was A$85 million (US$63 million) in the year to June 30, 1997, down from A$102.2 million a year ago.
"This reflects approximately A$50 million of higher depreciation and interest expenses primarily arising from the completion of the Chullora printing facility," Fairfax said in its results statement.
The Chullora plant in Western Sydney was built for A$330 million over 1995 and 1996 to allow Fairfax to print more colour photographs in its newspapers.
Net profit after abnormals fell 15.4 percent to A$74 million after abnormal losses of A$11 million for redundancy and restructure costs.
Despite the profit slide, it was within market estimates.

"It was a good result. It does not look like a good result, but it is," said one Sydney-based analyst. Analysts had forecast a pre-abnormal net profit between A$75.1 million to A$99.4 million, with a median forecast of A$90.3 million.
The current 1997/98 year had started stronger the previous year, Fairfax finance director John Greaves told Reuters.

Asked if first-half profit would be higher, Greaves said: "I would be surprised if it isn't..." but added although local data pointed to a economic lift, this had still not come. "It's a bit patchy. We are not in a position to say 'here we go'."
"The economy is still stagnant," he said.
Overall 1996/97 advertising volumes at Fairfax's The Sydney Morning Herald, The Australian Financial Review and The Age daily newspapers fell two percent.
"Classified advertising volumes were down by about two percent, mainly due to the lower real estate volumes offset by improvements in employment and motor," Fairfax said.
Fairfax is seen as a takeover target if the Australian government loosens current cross-media ownership rules, which are currently under consideration.
"I really don't know when that is coming out," Greaves said.
The Liberal-National party government ordered a review of the current rules after winning office in March 1996.
Australia's richest man, Kerry Packer, who owns 15 percent of Fairfax through his media empire Publishing & Broadcasting Ltd is seen a likely buyer of Fairfax if ownership laws change.
Fairfax shares closed one cent down at A$3.18 compared with A$3.21 before the results annoucement late in the afternoon.
